post_text:
Distributed locks in Redis felt like an elegant, lightweight shield against race conditions.

I was supremely confident that our short TTL would guarantee double-payouts were mathematically impossible across our cluster.

During a high-concurrency flash sale, a Stop-The-World JVM garbage collection pause suspended our primary settlement worker for twelve seconds.

The distributed lock expired silently in Redis while the JVM thread was frozen mid-transaction. When the GC pause cleared, the worker awoke and wrote the settlement to the primary database, totally oblivious that a secondary worker had already claimed the lock and executed the payout.

Millions of dollars in duplicate transactions flooded our financial ledgers while our Redis metrics showed green checkmarks across the board.

I had relied on transient, time-based locks to orchestrate safety instead of enforcing hard immutability at the storage engine level.

What I learned:

A distributed lock without a fencing token or database constraint is just an expensive, brittle illusion of safety.
